303	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
304	
305	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
307	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
308	
309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
342	
343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
349	
350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
353	
354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
355	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.

375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.

456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each

569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. 574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. ## Adversarial pass (process output)

The conclusion below is a recommendation/plan ("commission a diagnostic pass, prioritize architecture fixes"), so the Phase 5 adversarial technique is **pre-mortem** (not inversion) per the pre-mortem-vs-inversion decision rule.

**Recompute.** Trade-off totals (weights × scores, re-added independently of the C5 prose): buy faster runners = 10+6+16+4+6+15+10 = **67**; increase fleet concurrency = 10+6+16+8+9+10+10 = **69**; parallelize/shard tests-and-build = 25+12+8+16+15+20+4 = **100**; cache dependencies/builds = 20+15+16+12+12+15+8 = **98**; fast-feedback/full-gate split = 20+12+12+20+12+25+6 = **107**; fix flaky tests = 15+12+8+8+12+15+4 = **74**. Maximum possible = (5+3+4+4+3+5+2)×5 = **130**. All six totals recompute to the values C5 states. Amdahl illustrative bracket: p=0.30 → floor = 47×(1−0.30) = **14.1 min**; p=0.70 → floor = 47×(1−0.70) = **14.1 min... correction below.**

Correction on the second illustrative figure: floor = 47×(1−p), so for p=0.70, floor = 47×0.30 = **14.1 min**, and for p=0.30, floor = 47×0.70 = **32.9 min**. (The mapping in C3's third hop is: a *larger* accelerable fraction p produces a *smaller* floor. C3's text states "if 30 percent were fixed/serial the floor is ~14 min" — 30% fixed/serial means p=0.70 accelerable, floor=47×0.30=14.1 ✓ — and "if 70 percent were fixed/serial the floor is ~33 min" — 70% fixed/serial means p=0.30 accelerable, floor=47×0.70=32.9 ✓. Recomputed independently and confirmed to match C3 as written.)

**Sensitivity.** The single ground truth whose falsity (or rather, whose resolution) would flip the headline conclusion is **GT-1?** — the actual stage-by-stage composition of the 47 minutes (the compute-bound, parallel-eligible fraction *p*). It is `?`-marked. If instrumentation shows *p* is large (illustratively >80%) and flakiness/queueing are negligible, the recommendation flips toward a runner/fleet-capacity upgrade being the correctly-targeted primary fix rather than a complementary one — this is stated explicitly as the Falsification condition below. Weakest link per chain: C1 — the unmeasured *p* itself; C2 — the unmeasured dominant driver of batching; C3 — structurally solid, but practically inert without magnitude data; C4 — the unpriced growth assumption (A-7) plus its dependency on C1; C5 — scores generalize from typical CI architecture (A-11) rather than this org's measured data; C6 — inherits all of the above, dominated by the missing diagnostic.

**Rival.** *Headline (C6):* strongest rival — "just approve the runner purchase now; it's cheap, fast, and low-risk, so don't wait on a diagnostic." Ruled out by C5 (buy-faster-runners ranks lowest of six viable options, and the flip test shows no realistic single-criterion reweighting reverses this) and C4 (second-order moral-hazard/recurring-cost risk) — recorded in Abandoned Reasoning. *C1:* rival — "most CI time is typically CPU-bound test execution, so runners obviously help substantially" — live, not settled; shares the same evidence gap as C1's Inputs shortfall (closing the stage-breakdown gap settles both at once). *C2:* rival — "batching is driven mainly by duration, the plain reading of the scenario" — live, not settled, same gap. *C3:* rival — "there is no real floor; enough hardware could approach zero" — ruled out directly by GT-4 (Amdahl's mathematical asymptote), recorded in Abandoned Reasoning. *C4:* rival — "this org's engineering culture reliably maintains ownership/SLOs without an explicit process, so the moral-hazard risk won't materialize" — live, not settled; addressed procedurally below via pre-mortem Cluster A's tripwire rather than resolved. *C5:* rival — "this pipeline is dominated by one large, unshardable compute-bound stage, making parallelization moot and raw speed the only lever" — live, not settled; this is the named condition under which C5's ranking would need to be recomputed once data exists.

**Premise.** It is one year from now. Leadership approved the diagnostic-first recommendation and the follow-on architecture work — and CI pain and merge-batching are just as bad as they were the day this analysis was written. The plan has already failed.

**Causes** (unfiltered, generated from four stakeholder viewpoints — the individual contributor, the platform/CI-owning engineer, engineering leadership, and finance):

1. (IC) The diagnostic ran, but nobody acted on its findings — the report sat in a doc no one revisited.
2. (IC) The fast-feedback/full-gate split shipped, but the "full gate" quietly became a second blocking requirement developers still wait on, recreating the original wait.
3. (platform engineer) Test/build parallelization work was scoped but deprioritized every sprint in favor of feature work, since it carried no hard deadline.
4. (platform engineer) Dependency/build caching was added but invalidated incorrectly, producing intermittent false-pass/false-fail results that eroded trust in CI faster than the old, slow-but-honest pipeline did.
5. (leadership) Leadership funded the diagnostic *and* the runner purchase in parallel "to be safe," and the runner spend became the reflexive answer again the next time pain resurfaced, because it is the easiest lever to approve.
6. (leadership) No SLO or accountable owner was assigned for CI pipeline duration after the initial fix, so the same ownerless drift that produced the original 47-minute pipeline recurred.
7. (finance) The recurring runner-tier spend was approved but its effect was never tracked, so the organization cannot tell whether it reduced batching or not.
8. (IC) The codebase and test suite grew faster than anticipated; even after parallelization, the fixed/serial floor identified in C3 grew in absolute terms, so pain returned within the year.
9. (platform engineer) Flaky tests were never assigned an owner, so the retry tax persisted even after the other fixes shipped.
10. (leadership) The diagnostic instrumentation was built once as a one-off report and never kept as a live dashboard, so visibility was lost again within months.

**Clusters:**

- **Cluster A — No ownership/no SLO** (causes 3, 6, 9, 10; bears on C4, C6). Root: nobody is accountable for CI pipeline health as an ongoing property, so any fix decays.
- **Cluster B — Fix theater** (causes 1, 2, 4; bears on C2, C5, C6). Root: the recommended fixes were nominally implemented but not implemented well enough to change developer experience.
- **Cluster C — Old habit wins** (causes 5, 7; bears on C4, C5). Root: absent a decision discipline, the organization reverts to the easiest-to-approve lever rather than the most effective one.
- **Cluster D — Growth outpaces the fix** (cause 8; bears on C3, C4). Root: a one-time fix erodes as the codebase grows if not paired with a recurring review.

**Disposition:**

- Cluster A — **Plan change**: name an accountable owner for CI pipeline health and set a duration SLO as a condition of approving *any* fix, not as an afterthought. Triage: **Fatal** (an ownerless fix reliably decays to the original state, defeating the whole recommendation). Tripwire: no named owner and no CI-duration SLO exist 60 days after the diagnostic report ships — observed by the engineering manager who commissioned it.
- Cluster B — **Plan change**: require the diagnostic's findings and the shipped fixes to be reviewed against actual telemetry (batching rate, duration distribution) one full release cycle after launch, not assumed successful. Triage: **Costly but survivable**. Tripwire: telemetry shows the batching rate has not dropped within one release cycle after the fast-feedback split ships — observed by whoever owns the CI dashboard.
- Cluster C — **Accepted risk with mitigation**: allow a small, capped, low-regret fleet-concurrency spend (trade-off option B) to proceed in parallel with the diagnostic as a pressure-release valve, explicitly labeled as not the primary fix; the mitigation is Cluster A's owner/SLO preventing it from becoming the default answer again. Triage: **Costly but survivable**. Tripwire: a second runner-tier upgrade is proposed within 12 months without an accompanying diagnostic update — observed by finance/leadership reviewing recurring infra spend.
- Cluster D — **Plan change**: treat the fix as requiring a recurring (e.g., quarterly) CI-health review tied to the codebase/test-suite growth trajectory, not a one-time project. Triage: **Fatal if unaddressed at the process level**, tolerable within a one-year window if a review cadence is set now. Tripwire: CI duration trends back above the pain threshold that originally caused batching, measured quarterly — observed by the CI pipeline owner named under Cluster A.

**Falsification.** This analysis's conclusion is false if a stage-by-stage timing breakdown, once obtained, shows that the compute-bound, parallel-ineligible fraction of the 47 minutes is large (illustratively, dominates over ~80% of duration) **and** flakiness and queueing wait are negligible contributors — in that specific case, buying faster (or more) runners would be the correctly-targeted primary fix, not merely a complementary one.

FP_EOF
echo done

# Presented Analysis

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given a 47-minute CI pipeline that is causing developers to batch merges, is purchasing faster runners the right intervention — or is it treating a symptom while the actual driver(s) of both the duration and the batching behavior remain unaddressed?

**Success criteria:**
- The recommendation states, for the compute-bound and non-compute-bound portions of the 47 minutes, which portion "buy faster runners" can and cannot address.
- The recommendation addresses the batching *behavior* specifically (not only the raw minute count), naming the candidate drivers that a hardware purchase does and does not touch.
- The recommendation states whether a theoretical floor on pipeline duration exists and, if so, what governs it.
- The recommendation names the second-order risks of a hardware-only fix (cost trajectory, organizational incentive effects).
- The recommendation compares "buy faster runners" against concrete alternative interventions on stated criteria, not by assertion.
- The recommendation names the specific unknowns leadership must resolve before committing spend, and proposes how to resolve them.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

### Companion-technique inputs feeding this table

**Fishbone (default six-category set — People, Process, Technology and Tools, Environment, Information, Resources)**, brainstorming candidate drivers of the 47 minutes and the batching behavior:

| Category | Candidate causes | Discriminating observation |
|---|---|---|
| People | No single owner accountable for CI pipeline speed/health | No clean single observation — inferred from the absence of any CI-duration SLO or named owner, an organizational-structure fact rather than a technical measurement |
| Process | Pipeline stages may run serially rather than in parallel; pipeline may be an all-or-nothing blocking gate; flaky tests may be auto-retried without root-cause triage | Inspect the CI config's job dependency graph: stages that could fan out (lint, unit tests, build) but are chained sequentially confirms this |
| Technology and Tools | Runner hardware tier; no dependency/build caching configured; no test sharding configured; CI provider concurrency limits | Compare wall time of the install/build step across two consecutive runs with unchanged dependencies — if it doesn't drop, caching is absent or ineffective |
| Environment | Shared runner contention with other teams/projects; network latency to package registries; cold container/VM start overhead | Compare "time submitted" vs. "time started running" in CI logs — nontrivial wait indicates fleet contention rather than per-run compute time |
| Information | No dashboard/visibility into stage-by-stage timing, flake rate, or queue wait; "47 minutes" itself may not be a consistently defined figure (mean vs. p95, which branch) | Pull CI history for retry counts/re-run rate over recent runs — a high rate of automatic re-runs before green is the tell for flakiness specifically |
| Resources | Budget/headcount for platform engineering may be low relative to the pain, making a purchase (no dedicated engineering time required) organizationally easier to approve than re-architecture | No clean single observation — inferred from which fix leadership defaulted to proposing |

**Five-whys (causal mode)** on the symptom "developers are batching merges to avoid the pipeline":
Why(1) — triggering the pipeline costs 47 minutes per run, multiplied across the team's workflow when run per-PR. Counterfactual: without the 47-minute cost, would batching still happen? No, per the scenario's own framing — necessary, drill further.
Why(2a) — a 47-minute cost only translates into "avoid running it" if the pipeline is a synchronous blocking gate developers must wait through before merging (untested belief A-10). Counterfactual: if the pipeline were non-blocking, would batching still occur to avoid the 47 minutes? Plausibly less — both duration and blocking design are necessary conditions.
Why(2b) — 47 minutes is long enough to force a context switch (a developer cannot productively wait and must return to it later, paying a re-entry cost) — a well-documented general cost of interruptions in knowledge work, though the specific threshold for this team is unverified.
Why(3) — the organization tolerates this combination because (candidates, unverified) no CI-duration SLO/owner exists to check stage accretion over time, and/or the pipeline was never re-architected as the codebase grew. **Stop rule applied:** drilling further ("why does no SLO exist") moves into general organizational-prioritization territory outside this analysis's actionable scope — recorded as context for pre-mortem Cluster A instead.
Root-cause verdicts: "47-minute duration" = contributing condition (necessary but not independently sufficient), within control; "synchronous blocking-gate design" = root-cause candidate, within control, corrective = fast-feedback/full-gate split; "no CI-duration ownership/SLO" = root-cause candidate, within control at the leadership level; "codebase/test growth outpacing pipeline architecture" = contributing condition, partially within control.

**Inversion** on "buying faster runners is the right call": necessary preconditions, each tagged load-bearing (LB) or not —
P1 (LB): a significant fraction of the 47 minutes is compute/IO-bound and parallel-eligible on the upgraded resource.
P2 (LB): flaky-test retries are not the dominant time driver.
P3 (LB): queueing/fleet-contention wait is not the dominant complaint, or is separately addressed.
P4 (not LB): the organization still pursues architectural fixes after the purchase rather than treating it as solved.
P5 (LB): codebase/test-suite growth is slow enough that the benefit isn't quickly eroded.
All five are unverified given facts and enter the table below as untested beliefs (P1→A-2, P2→A-8, P3 folded into A-4/A-8, P4→A-6, P5→A-7).

### Classified Assumptions Table

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| A-1: Faster runners will reduce the 47-minute pipeline duration | convention (embedded in leadership's framing) | Explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — true only for the compute/IO-bound, non-serialized fraction; magnitude unknown (GT-6) | unverified — flagged |
| A-2: The 47 minutes is predominantly CPU/compute-bound | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — no stage-breakdown data supplied; could equally be I/O, fixed-cost, or serialized | unverified — flagged |
| A-3: Pipeline steps are already maximally parallelized | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — unknown; common pattern is more serial than necessary | unverified — flagged |
| A-4: Developers are batching merges solely because of the 47-minute duration | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — could equally be flaky-retry unpredictability, queueing wait, or blocking-gate design | unverified — flagged |
| A-5: There is no hard floor on pipeline duration; enough hardware could approach zero | untested belief | Verify | Discard — contradicted directly by GT-4 (Amdahl's Law) | source: GT-4 |
| A-6: Buying faster runners is a low-risk decision with no organizational side effects | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — second-order analysis (C4) identifies a moral-hazard risk to fixing the underlying architecture | unverified — flagged |
| A-7: The codebase/test-suite growth trajectory is such that a one-time hardware upgrade's benefit will not erode quickly | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — no growth-rate data supplied; typical pattern is growth outpacing one-time hardware bumps | unverified — flagged |
| A-8: Flaky tests/retries are not a meaningful contributor to the 47 minutes | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — retry rate not supplied | unverified — flagged |
| A-9: "Faster" runners and "more" runners are the same lever | convention (conflation embedded in the phrase "faster runners") | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard as stated — distinct levers addressing distinct problems | source: GT-8 |
| A-10: The CI pipeline is a synchronous, blocking gate developers must wait through before merging | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible given "avoid it" framing but not confirmed; changes the shape of the fast-feedback intervention if false | unverified — flagged |
| A-11: This pipeline's architecture is not a significant outlier from typical CI pipelines | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — the C5 trade-off scoring depends on this; an atypical pipeline (e.g., one unshardable dominant stage) would change the ranking | unverified — flagged |
| A-12: Leadership will accept a short (1–2 week) diagnostic delay before committing capital spend | untested belief | Verify or flag unverified | Challenge — organizational-feasibility assumption, not confirmed | unverified — flagged |

FP_EOF
echo done

- **GT-3?** Leadership's proposed intervention is to purchase faster CI runners — unverified: stated as a premise of this scenario; whether "faster" means per-unit speed, fleet concurrency, or both is not specified.
- **GT-4** Amdahl's Law: S(s) = 1/(1 − p + p/s), where p is the fraction of execution time that benefits from a speedup of factor s; as s→∞, S(s) asymptotically approaches 1/(1−p) — the non-accelerable fraction sets a hard ceiling on total achievable speedup — source: Wikipedia, "Amdahl's law"; read-at-source: the "Formula" and "Critical Insight About Maximum Speedup" sections, quoted directly ("Even with infinite acceleration... the speedup asymptotically approaches 1/(1-p)").
- **GT-5** A CI pipeline's wall-clock duration is a sum of heterogeneous stages — environment/container provisioning, dependency resolution/download, source checkout, compile/build, test execution (itself possibly serial and/or parallel, with retries on failure), artifact packaging/upload, and any sequential quality gates — each of which may be CPU-bound, I/O/network-bound, fixed-cost regardless of hardware, or serialized by dependency or policy — provenance: definitional/architectural (general CI/CD system structure), not a disputed empirical figure.
- **GT-6** Faster CPU/memory/disk hardware reduces wall-clock time only for the portions of a job that are compute/IO-bound on that specific resource and not blocked by external network latency, fixed-cost operations, or serialization/sequencing constraints — provenance: definitional, direct logical corollary of GT-4 + GT-5.
- **GT-7** Non-deterministic ("flaky") test failures that trigger automatic retries add wall-clock time proportional to retry count times the execution/timeout duration of the retried tests; this added time is a function of test determinism and retry policy, not of CPU clock speed — provenance: definitional/logical corollary of GT-6.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Approve the runner purchase now without a diagnostic

**What was tried:** Considered the straightforward reading of leadership's request — approve the purchase immediately since it is cheap, fast to ship, and low-implementation-risk relative to alternatives.

**Why abandoned:** The trade-off analysis (C5) ranks this option lowest of six viable interventions (67/130), and the flip test shows no realistic single-criterion reweighting reverses that ranking; the second-order analysis (C4) additionally identifies a moral-hazard risk (relieving visible pain removes pressure to fix the real driver) and a recurring/escalating cost trajectory.

**What it ruled out:** This is the strongest rival to the headline conclusion (C6) and is ruled out by C4 and C5 together — a reader considering "just buy the runners" does not need to re-derive this comparison.

### Dead End: There is no real floor; sufficient hardware could approach zero duration

**What was tried:** Considered whether an unbounded hardware budget could, in principle, drive pipeline duration toward zero, making the entire "floor" concern moot.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted directly by GT-4 (Amdahl's Law): as speedup s→∞, S(s) asymptotically approaches 1/(1−p), a finite bound whenever any fraction p<1 is non-accelerable — a mathematical necessity, not an empirical claim requiring further evidence.

**What it ruled out:** The rival to C3's structural claim; ruled out by GT-4 alone, which is why C3 is rated HIGH rather than MEDIUM despite the floor's magnitude being unmeasured.

**What was tried:** Considered reframing the batching behavior as an intentional strategy (analogous to a release train) rather than reactive avoidance, which would change the problem essence entirely.

**Why abandoned:** The given scenario explicitly frames it as reactive avoidance ("developers have started batching merges to avoid it"); inventing a benign alternative interpretation would contradict the stated premise (GT-2?) and violate the Input Contract's instruction to treat unstated details as unknowns rather than invent favorable facts.

**What it ruled out:** An alternative framing of the Problem Essence; ruled out by GT-2? as given.

**What was tried:** Considered whether simply adding more concurrent runners (addressing queueing wait) would be sufficient on its own, without touching compute speed, caching, or test architecture.

**What it ruled out:** A narrower rival to C5's ranking; ruled out by C5 itself in combination with GT-8.

**What was tried:** Considered leaving the pipeline and the batching workaround as-is, treating the current equilibrium as acceptable.

**Why abandoned:** Knocked out by the trade-off's must-have that any viable option must plausibly reduce the pain driving batching; doing nothing cannot satisfy this by definition.

**What it ruled out:** Eliminated from C5's option set before scoring, per the trade-off procedure's required inclusion-then-knockout step for the status quo.

**Why abandoned:** No cost, pricing, or growth data was supplied by the scenario, and the Input Contract explicitly requires treating unstated details as unknowns to flag rather than invent; fabricated figures would misrepresent this analysis's actual confidence.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not approve "buy faster runners" as the primary or sole fix. Commission a short (1–2 week) diagnostic pass — a stage-by-stage pipeline timing breakdown, the flaky/retry rate, current runner queue-wait and utilization, and the current state of caching and parallelization — and act on what it shows; in parallel, default to the higher-ranked architectural levers (fast-feedback/full-gate split, test-and-build parallelization, dependency caching), which this analysis's reasoned trade-off found to dominate hardware spend across most plausible scenarios (chain C6).

**Key insight:** "47 minutes" and "developers are batching merges" are two different problems that a runner upgrade only partially and unreliably touches. Amdahl's Law guarantees a hard floor on pipeline duration that no hardware purchase can cross, and the specific batching behavior leadership wants eliminated may be driven by flakiness, queueing, or the pipeline's blocking-gate design rather than by raw compute duration — none of which "faster runners" reliably fixes (chains C1, C2, C3).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** A runner upgrade is the lowest-effort, fastest-to-ship option among those examined, and it is not being ruled out permanently — it may be the right complementary move once the compute-bound fraction is actually measured. The diagnostic-first path costs a small delay and some engineering time that spend-averse leadership may resist, and a capped, low-regret fleet-concurrency purchase can run in parallel with the diagnostic as a pressure-release valve without becoming the default answer, provided the ownership/SLO gap identified in the adversarial pass is closed at the same time (chain C5).

Obtaining that data — the diagnostic pass this recommendation itself calls for — would let this Conclusion move to HIGH, or, per the Falsification condition in the adversarial pass record above, reverse the specific sub-conclusion that a runner upgrade is not the primary fix.
